lessons.title: Horizontal vs Vertical Scaling
lessons.subtitle: Understanding how systems grow — and the trade-offs each approach demands.
lessons.insight: Most real systems don't pick one and ignore the other — they start vertical for simplicity, then shift horizontal once demand outgrows what a single box can handle.

lessons.title: Latency, Throughput & Availability
lessons.subtitle: The three pillars of system observability — if you can't measure these, you can't operate.
lessons.insight: Optimizing one in isolation is easy. The hard part is the trade-off — pushing throughput up often pushes latency up too.

lessons.title: CAP Theorem & Trade-offs
lessons.subtitle: When the network fails, you must choose — and there is no middle ground.
lessons.insight: During a network partition you only get two of three: consistency, availability, partition tolerance. Most real systems pick AP or CP and design around it.

lessons.title: Core Concepts of Load Balancing
lessons.subtitle: Distribute traffic, eliminate single points of failure, and scale without downtime.
lessons.insight: A load balancer isn't just traffic distribution — it's what turns a single point of failure into a resilient cluster.

lessons.title: Design Requirements & Estimating Resource Needs
lessons.subtitle: Turning vague product goals into concrete, quantifiable engineering constraints.
lessons.insight: Before you design anything, you need real numbers — QPS, storage growth, read/write ratio. Vague requirements produce vague architectures.

lessons.title: Webhooks vs. Polling: Choosing a Communication Pattern
lessons.subtitle: How a system finds out about changes it didn't initiate.
lessons.insight: Polling asks "anything new?" on a timer. Webhooks flip the model — the system tells you the moment something changes.
